In the kasba school near Sagar, the cricket team was really a group of five boys who had grown up in the same lane. Vishal, fifteen, had moved there from another village in June. He bowled better than most of them, but they picked him last, if at all.
On Saturday, Rajni, the sports captain, watched it happen. When Deepak, one of the five, dropped two easy catches, the others slapped his back. "Unlucky, yaar." When Vishal misfielded once, the same boys groaned loudly. "Village-boy hands."
"You're from a village too," Vishal muttered, but no one heard.
He walked home the long way, kicking stones. His mother asked if the match went well. "Fine," he said, and went straight to the roof, where he bowled at the water tank alone until it was dark.
On Monday, Rajni wrote the fielding errors in the scorebook for every player, with names.

qa.q: How many boys made up the cricket group?
qa.a: It was a group of five boys who had grown up in the same lane.

qa.q: What does Vishal bowling alone at the water tank until dark suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and shut out, still loving the game but not wanting to talk about how unfairly he had been treated.

qa.q: How might Rajni's scorebook change things for Vishal?
qa.a: Writing every player's fielding errors with names makes the record the same for everyone, so Deepak's dropped catches and Vishal's misfield are judged by one rule.

qa.q: What was it like for Vishal to hear 'Village-boy hands' after Deepak was told 'Unlucky, yaar'?
qa.a: For Vishal it showed that the group excused its own and judged him harshly for less, which is why he muttered that they were from a village too.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy outside a village cricket clique watching members excuse each other while he is judged harshly for smaller slips.

Swati, you asked why I started that hostel help-desk thing. Okay. I'm Neelam, second year, and it began with me just noticing.
In our hostel, when a senior had spare notes, they went to juniors from their own state. When the canteen needed a student helper, the manager hired "someone from back home." When a first-year from Manipur asked for help with the library portal, three people said they were busy, and ten minutes later helped a boy from their own district.
Nobody was being cruel. It just flowed that way, like water downhill. I did it too. My first instinct was always to help people who spoke my language.
So I started saying it out loud at hostel meetings: "Help keeps going to our own people." People were uncomfortable. But then we set up a shared notes shelf and a sign-up sheet for helpers, open to anyone. Last week the Manipur girl ran it.

qa.q: Who did the canteen manager hire as a student helper?
qa.a: The manager hired "someone from back home."

qa.q: What made Neelam feel the pattern wasn't about cruelty?
qa.a: Neelam noticed it just flowed that way, like water downhill, and even caught the same urge to help people who spoke the same language first.

qa.q: What did Neelam do after noticing the pattern, and why was naming it important?
qa.a: Neelam said it out loud at hostel meetings, which led to a shared notes shelf and an open sign-up sheet, since change began once people could see the pattern.

qa.q: How might the first-year from Manipur have seen the hostel before and after?
qa.a: At first she was turned away while others were helped, which likely felt lonely and unfair; running the shelf later suggests she felt included and trusted.

grounding: A student notices help, jobs and trust flowing towards people from the same region, and naming it becomes the first step towards fairness.

I'm Kiran, and I share a lab bench with Salma in our engineering college in Coimbatore. This semester I watched her do something unusual.
Our department's paid research assistant posts went to six students. Salma pulled up the list on her phone one evening and showed me. All six had gone to the same two schools as the professors. Then she scrolled back: last year, the same.
She didn't sound angry, more puzzled. "The professors probably trust people who remind them of their own school," she said. "Maybe they don't even know they're doing it."
I don't know how nervous she was, but her hands were tight around her phone when she asked the head of department, politely, if the posts could have a written application and a scoring sheet next time.
He frowned, then said he'd think about it. This month's notice board has a form on it. Salma just pointed at it and smiled.

qa.q: How many students got the paid research assistant posts?
qa.a: The posts went to six students.

qa.q: What did Salma seem to think was behind the pattern?
qa.a: She seemed to think the professors trusted students who reminded them of their own schools, perhaps without realising it, which is why she sounded puzzled rather than angry.

qa.q: What did Salma ask the head of department for, and why was it a fair step?
qa.a: She asked for a written application and a scoring sheet, so the posts would be judged on clear criteria rather than on familiarity.

qa.q: How does Kiran see what Salma did?
qa.a: Kiran watched closely and noticed her tight grip on the phone, but is careful not to claim to know how nervous she really was.

grounding: Told by a classmate, it shows a student noticing that opportunities flow to people from the same schools and naming the pattern to make it fairer.

At the block development office in a kasba near Dhule, Gargi, twenty-five, had to choose ten farmers for a free drip-irrigation training. By noon, most names on her list came from her own village and the one next to it; people she knew, who had phoned her directly.
She looked at the list and felt uneasy. Were these really the best choices, or just the familiar ones?
She wrote three rules on a sheet: small landholding, a water problem, and nobody from the same family twice. Then she asked Harsha, the field assistant, "Can you bring me names from the villages across the river? I don't know anyone there."
Harsha came back with fourteen names. Gargi scored everyone using the same sheet. Four from her village stayed on the list. Six new names joined it.
One of them, an old woman, came to the office just to see the list, and touched it twice.

qa.q: How many new names joined Gargi's list after she used the sheet?
qa.a: Six new names joined it.

qa.q: What was Gargi worried about when she looked at her first list?
qa.a: She worried that the names were chosen because they were familiar, people from her own and the next village who had phoned her, not because they were the best choices.

qa.q: Which steps did Gargi take to make the selection fairer?
qa.a: She wrote three clear rules, asked Harsha to bring names from villages across the river where she knew no one, and scored everyone on the same sheet.

qa.q: What might the old woman's touching the list twice suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she could hardly believe she was included, and perhaps that people like her had often been left out of such lists before.

grounding: It shows a young officer using clear criteria and reaching out to people unlike herself, checking she would make the same call regardless of group.

I'm Maria, and I teach tuition classes to five kids in our building in Goa. On Tuesday, Mr. Fernandes from upstairs came down and told Nitin's mother that Nitin had broken his window with a ball. Nitin was sent home crying, grounded for a week.
Simran, nine, watched from the table. After he left, she said, "Nitin must be a bad boy. Good children don't get punished."
"We don't know yet what happened," I said.
"But he got punished, so he did something," she said, as if that settled it.
On Thursday, Mr. Fernandes came back, embarrassed. It was a pigeon that cracked the glass, not a ball. I watched Simran's face; she looked confused, frowning at her notebook. I can't know what she thought. She didn't say anything, but on Friday she lent Nitin her best pencil.

qa.q: What actually cracked Mr. Fernandes's window?
qa.a: It was a pigeon that cracked the glass, not a ball.

qa.q: Why did Simran feel sure Nitin must be a bad boy?
qa.a: She believed that good children don't get punished, so the punishment itself seemed like proof that he had done something wrong.

qa.q: How could Maria help Simran think about this after the truth came out?
qa.a: Maria could ask Simran what she thinks now about Nitin and the pigeon, and let her notice for herself that sometimes people are punished for things they didn't do.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel when Simran lends him her best pencil?
qa.a: Nitin might feel a little comforted, especially after being blamed and grounded for something a pigeon did.

grounding: Told by a tutor, it shows a girl assuming a punished boy must have done something bad, because fairness feels like the rule of the world.

In the boys' hostel common room at the coaching centre, the news was everywhere by dinner: someone had taken Faizan's new cycle from outside the library.
Mohit, sixteen, shrugged over his dal. "He left it with a cheap lock. What did he expect? If you show off a new cycle, you're asking for it."
Sudha ma'am, the warden, was passing with the attendance register. She stopped. "Your cycle is outside the same library, Mohit. What lock does it have?"
Mohit paused. "The same kind, ma'am. But mine's old."
"So if it were stolen tomorrow, would you have asked for it?"
He opened his mouth and shut it again. Blaming Faizan had felt so much safer; if it was Faizan's fault, it couldn't happen to him.
Sudha ma'am said quietly, "The one who took it is responsible. Faizan's just the one who lost it." Then she went to find Faizan, who hadn't come down for dinner.

qa.q: Where was Faizan's cycle taken from?
qa.a: From outside the library.

qa.q: Why did blaming Faizan feel comfortable to Mohit?
qa.a: If the theft was Faizan's fault for showing off, then Mohit could believe it wouldn't happen to him, even though his own cycle had the same kind of lock.

qa.q: What question from Sudha ma'am made Mohit stop, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked whether he would have 'asked for it' if his own cycle were stolen tomorrow, which made him see his reasoning only protected himself.

qa.q: How might Faizan be feeling while the others discuss his cycle at dinner?
qa.a: Faizan, who hadn't come down, is likely upset and perhaps embarrassed, and hearing he 'asked for it' would add shame to the loss.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy blaming a classmate for a theft, a belief that protects his own sense of being safe, and a warden gently challenging it.

When he mentioned it to a batchmate, the answer came fast: "You must have annoyed them somehow. They don't pick on random people."

Aadhya, from his lab batch, noticed he had skipped three meals. She sat beside him on the stairs. "It's not your fault," she said. "Nobody deserves that."

At a cousin's wedding in a Pune banquet hall, Dhruv, twenty, sat at the edge of the relatives' table in a kurta that hung loose after two months in bed with a long illness. He had lost a semester.
Manoj Mama leaned across the gulab jamuns. "At your age, illness doesn't come from nowhere. Late nights, outside food, isn't it? You must have done something."
A few aunties nodded. Someone added, "Everything happens for a reason."
Dhruv's face went hot. He had eaten at home, slept early, done everything right. But he said nothing. He looked at his plate until the music started, then went and stood by the parking lot.
His mother found him there. "It wasn't your fault," she said quietly. "Mama doesn't know." Dhruv nodded but didn't answer. On the drive home he kept the window down, letting the noise of the road fill the silence.

qa.a: Two months in bed with a long illness.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv say nothing to Manoj Mama?

qa.a: She went to find him and told him quietly that it wasn't his fault, which counters the shame the relatives' words added.

qa.q: How might Manoj Mama see his own comment?
qa.a: Manoj Mama probably thinks he is being wise or caring, not realising that his words add shame to Dhruv's pain and push him into silence.

grounding: It shows a student who suffered a long illness being told he must have caused it, which adds shame and silences him.

The hailstorm lasted twenty minutes and flattened Akash's whole wheat field outside the village near Bhopal. Next morning, at the tea stall, someone said, "His father fought with the temple committee. What goes around comes around." Others nodded.
Aparna, twenty-six, the agriculture extension worker, put down her glass. "The hail fell on his field and on the Rathores' field too. Did they fight with anyone?" Nobody answered.
She walked to Akash's house. He was sitting in the yard, not speaking. She didn't say it was destiny or a lesson. She said, "This was bad luck, and it's heavy. I'm here." She sat with him for an hour, then helped him photograph the damage and fill the relief form at the block office.
Back at the office, she pushed for the hailstorm survey to cover every farm in the area, not just the big ones.

Last year, in Class 10, I skipped sports day because of a school bag. I'm Kamal, and I know how that sounds.
My old bag had torn, so Appa gave me his old office bag, brown and stiff with a big buckle. "A proper bag for my son," he said proudly. The first day I carried it, I was sure the whole school was staring. On the stairs I held it behind my legs. I imagined people laughing about it at lunch.
When sports day came, you had to carry your things to the ground. I told Amma I had a stomach ache. I stayed home.
Rukmini, my cousin, who's in my class, told me later that nobody had mentioned my bag at all. "Half of them were worrying about their own shoes," she said.
Now I look at that bag and feel a bit silly. The only person who stared at it all year was me.

qa.a: Appa gave him his old office bag, brown and stiff with a big buckle.

subtype: Speaking up in class or interviews [Actor]
passage:
Week one, Monday. In the first sociology seminar at his Delhi college, Divyansh, nineteen, answered a question and called a famous thinker by the wrong name. Someone at the back chuckled. His ears burned all day.
Week three, Thursday. He hadn't spoken since. Twice he had a good point about the reading ready, his hand half lifted, and both times he put it down. They'll remember the name thing, he thought. They'll think I'm a fraud.
Week five, Tuesday. In the canteen, Mohit, who sat beside him in every seminar, said, "You barely talk in class. You okay?"
Divyansh blurted, "After I messed up that name?"
Mohit frowned. "What name?"
He genuinely had no idea. Divyansh sat there with his samosa going cold, thinking about five weeks of silence over something nobody else remembered.

qa.q: What did Divyansh get wrong in the first seminar?
qa.a: He called a famous thinker by the wrong name.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh keep putting his hand down in week three?
qa.a: He feared that classmates still remembered his slip and would think he was a fraud, so speaking again felt too risky.

qa.q: What could Divyansh try in the next seminar after the canteen talk?
qa.a: He could raise his hand and make one of the points he has been saving, now knowing that even Mohit had forgotten the slip.

qa.q: How did Mohit see Divyansh's silence during those weeks?
qa.a: Mohit noticed Divyansh barely talking and was concerned, but had no memory of the name slip at all.

grounding: Across three beats it shows a student staying silent for weeks over a slip that classmates barely noticed or quickly forgot.

subtype: Speaking up in class or interviews [Actor]
passage:
Nilesh, you're dreading the campus interview because you might stumble on a word? Let your Gurleen Bua tell you something from when I was twenty.
My first job interview was at a bank in Ludhiana. When the manager asked my name, I said my surname first, then my first name, then my surname again. I went red. Three people on the panel. I was sure they'd laugh about it at lunch for a week.
For the rest of the interview I barely spoke, just short answers. I thought I'd ruined everything.
Two years later, I ended up working in that same bank. I asked the manager, a kind man, if he remembered my interview. He thought hard and said, "Were you the girl who asked about the training programme?" He remembered my one good question. Not the stumble.

qa.q: At which bank did Gurleen Bua have her first job interview?
qa.a: It was at a bank in Ludhiana.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen Bua give only short answers after mixing up her name?
qa.a: She was sure the panel would laugh about it for a week, so she was afraid of making another mistake and held back.

qa.q: What could Nilesh take from Bua's story before the campus interview?
qa.a: Nilesh could keep in mind that a small stumble is rarely remembered, and focus on asking or answering one good question instead of going quiet.

qa.q: How did the manager remember Gurleen's interview?
qa.a: He didn't remember the stumble at all; he remembered her as the girl who asked about the training programme.

grounding: An elder recalls fearing her small interview slip would be remembered for weeks, when the manager recalled only her good question.
